extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (prosecution/review)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining patent-eligibility under 35 U.S.C. §101 for claims that implicate laws of nature, natural phenomena, and products of nature, including how and when to apply the markedly different characteristics analysis and related Step 2A/2B considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical formulas and scientific principles are non-statutory exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical formula such as the claimed Arrhenius equation is an exception like a scientific principle or natural phenomenon, and is non-statutory subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited include: (i) an algorithm for converting binary coded decimal to pure binary (Benson), (ii) a formula for computing an alarm limit (Flook), (iii) a formula describing certain electromagnetic standing wave phenomena (Mackay Radio & Tel.), and (iv) a mathematical formula for hedging (Bilski). The Supreme Court and Federal Circuit decisions treat basic mathematical equations like laws of nature or natural phenomena and therefore as patent-ineligible exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concepts relating to performing mathematical calculations are abstract ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that recite generating/transforming data by mathematical computation or organizing information through mathematical correlations are directed to abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Bancorp (managing life insurance policy values by performing calculations is the abstract idea of performing calculations/manipulating results), Digitech (generating data by manipulating existing information with mathematical formulas = organizing information through mathematical correlations). Other examples include algorithms for optimizing visits (In re Maucorps), calculating abnormal-condition parameters (In re Grams), and calculating differences between local and average data values (In re Abele). Such recitations are treated as abstract ideas in Step 2A analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws of nature and natural phenomena are judicial exceptions to §101
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws of nature and natural phenomena include naturally occurring principles/relations and nature-based products that are naturally occurring or that do not have markedly different characteristics compared to what occurs in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The basic tools of scientific and technological work (manifestations of laws of nature) are not patentable because they are part of the storehouse of knowledge (Funk Bros.). Examples identified by the courts include isolated DNA (Myriad), cloned farm animals (Roslin), correlations between non-coding and coding DNA regions (Genetic Techs.), correlations resulting from metabolism (Mayo), correlations of biomarkers to disease risk (Cleveland Clinic v. True Health), electromagnetism to transmit signals (O'Reilly v. Morse), bacterial qualities (Funk Bros.), primers (Ambry), chemical principles (Tilghman), and cffDNA existence (Ariosa). Not every claim describing a natural ability is directed to a law of nature; claims that recite concrete process steps (e.g., treating cancer with chemotherapy, cryopreserving hepatocytes) may be eligible if not focused on merely observing/detecting natural phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Products of nature exception (physical products that are natural or lack marked differences)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a law of nature or natural phenomenon is claimed as a physical product, the courts often treat it as a 'product of nature' exception to eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Products of nature include both naturally occurring products and non-naturally occurring products that lack markedly different characteristics from their natural counterparts. Synthetically replicated gene sequences that are structurally identical to natural counterparts remain ineligible (Ambry). Examples: isolated gene and cDNA (Myriad), cloned animals (Roslin), bacteria (Chakrabarty). Examiners should apply the markedly different characteristics analysis (MPEP §2106.04(c)) to nature-based product limitations to determine Step 2A. A claim to a nature-based product may encompass both eligible and ineligible embodiments under the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI); examiners should point this out and, if appropriate, recommend narrowing amendments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markedly different characteristics analysis is used to identify product-of-nature exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The markedly different characteristics analysis is part of Step 2A and compares the claimed nature-based product to its naturally occurring counterpart to determine whether the claimed product is a product of nature exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the nature-based product has markedly different characteristics from its natural counterpart, the limitation is not a product-of-nature exception and the claim is eligible at Step 2A (Pathway B) unless another exception is present. If the product does not exhibit markedly different characteristics, it is a product-of-nature exception (Step 2A: YES) and requires further Step 2B analysis to determine whether additional claim elements add significantly more. Markedly different characteristics can be expressed as differences in structure, function, and/or other properties, and are evaluated on a case-by-case basis based on the claim recitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply the markedly different characteristics analysis only to nature-based product limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: The markedly different characteristics analysis should be applied only to the nature-based product limitations in the claim, not to non-nature elements or entire claims that are not nature-based.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Care should be taken not to overextend the analysis to products that when viewed as a whole are not nature-based. Example distinctions: for a 'yogurt starter kit' claim, analyze only the Lactobacillus limitation for marked differences; container and instructions are not subject to this analysis but would be evaluated in Step 2B if the Lactobacillus is a product-of-nature exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markedly different analysis for product claims: apply to entire claimed product
rubrics_metrics.description: When the claim is to a nature-based product by itself (e.g., 'a Lactobacillus bacterium'), apply the markedly different characteristics analysis to the entire product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Chakrabarty: apply analysis to the entire claimed bacterium (e.g., genetically modified Pseudomonas with plasmids). For combinations that produce a resultant nature-based combination (e.g., probiotic composition of Lactobacillus and milk), analyze the resultant combination rather than individual components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markedly different analysis for product-by-process claims: focus on product characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: For product-by-process claims, the analysis turns on whether the nature-based product in the claim has markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §2113 for more on product-by-process claims. The key inquiry remains whether the claimed product differs markedly from natural counterparts, regardless of the recited process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markedly different analysis for process claims: generally not applied unless the claim is product-focused
rubrics_metrics.description: For a process claim, the general rule is that the markedly different characteristics analysis is not applied to nature-based products used in the process because the focus is on active process steps rather than products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: claims reciting fractionating, recovering, and cryopreserving hepatocytes were not subjected to the markedly different analysis because the claims were directed to a process. However, if a process claim is drafted so there is no substantive difference from a product claim (i.e., it effectively claims the product), then the marked-difference analysis should be applied (e.g., 'a method of providing an apple' focuses on the apple itself). Claims that merely detect naturally occurring substances (e.g., detecting cffDNA) may be directed to the natural phenomenon/product and be subject to product-of-nature analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to perform the markedly different characteristics analysis — selecting appropriate counterpart(s)
rubrics_metrics.description: Select the appropriate naturally occurring counterpart(s) to the claimed nature-based product; the comparison is to the counterpart in its natural state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the nature-based product is derived from a naturally occurring thing, the natural source is the counterpart (e.g., deoxyacid A derived from acid A → compare to acid A). Do not conflate the counterpart with adjacent natural material (e.g., compare a claimed gene to the gene, not to the whole chromosome). When multiple counterparts exist, compare to the closest naturally occurring counterpart based on examiner expertise (e.g., choose closest breed for a cloned sheep). For combinations without a natural counterpart, the closest counterparts may be the individual nature-based components (e.g., compare a claimed bacterial mixture to each species as it occurs in nature). If an examiner rejects on eligibility grounds, it is best practice to identify the selected counterpart in the Office action if not already clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to perform the markedly different characteristics analysis — identifying and evaluating characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Markedly different characteristics may be expressed as differences in structure, function, and/or other properties and are evaluated based on what is recited in the claim on a case-by-case basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claimed nature-based product is naturally occurring, no further marked-difference analysis is necessary (it falls under the product-of-nature exception). If it is not naturally occurring (e.g., created by human intervention), the examiner must identify appropriate characteristics for comparison and evaluate whether they are 'markedly different' from the natural counterpart. The evaluation depends on claim recitations and factual record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) and examiner best practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Under BRI, a nature-based product limitation may encompass both eligible and ineligible products; examiners should consider BRI when determining eligibility and recommend claim amendments where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a claim to a 'cloned giraffe' may cover embodiments with and without markedly different characteristics. If a claim is directed to a product of nature and is rejected as failing to encompass an inventive concept (Step 2B:NO), it is a best practice for the examiner to point out the BRI and recommend narrowing amendments to limit the claim to embodiments that are not directed to products of nature or are otherwise eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to use the streamlined eligibility analysis (MPEP §2106.06)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should consider whether the streamlined eligibility analysis is appropriate for claims that recite a nature-based product limitation but do not seek to tie up any judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim clearly does not tie up a judicial exception despite reciting a nature-based product limitation, it may be appropriate to use the streamlined eligibility pathway and avoid performing the markedly different characteristics analysis.
